ety.text: From Middle English oughte, aughte, aȝte, ahte, from Old English āhte, first and third person singular past tense of Old English āgan (“to own, possess”), equivalent to owe + -t. Cognate with Sanskrit ईश्वर (īśvará, “capable of, liable”).

ex: I ought to vote in the coming election.
You ought to always stand back from the edge of the platform.
Do you think we ought to leave now?
He ought to read the book; it was very good.
We ought to arrive by noon if we take the motorway, shouldn't we?

senses.d: A statement of what ought to be the case as contrasted with what is the case.
ex: Is there a fallacy involved in deriving an ought from a set of exclusively factual or descriptive premises?

fr:devoir.gl: must, to have to, should (as a requirement)

chain.g: to owe something, to be under obligation to and for something

ety.text: Inherited from Middle French debvoir, from Old French deveir, from Latin dēbēre (to owe; ought, must).
Inherited from Latin dēbēre (“to owe”). Cognate with Sicilian duviri.
Inherited from Old Spanish dever, from Latin dēbēre (“owe”). Cognates include English due and debt.

pt:dever.gl: should (indicates that an action is considered by the speaker to be obligatory)
